title: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 on AWS
text:
Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 on AWS
Today, we are announcing the availability of Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on Amazon Bedrock and Claude Platform on AWS. Claude Fable 5.2 is Anthropic’s most capable generally available model for technical work that raises the bar in coding and the sciences. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available through Anthropic’s verification programs for advanced work in cyber security and life sciences.
In this post, we cover what’s new in both models, why Fable 5.2 matters for your technical workloads, and how to get started building with the model on Amazon Bedrock.
Why Claude Fable 5.2
Fable 5.2 raises the bar on the hardest problems in coding, math, and science. It takes on ambiguous, multi-step work, verifies its own output, and can run unattended for hours to days. It interprets prompts, iterates, catches its own errors, and optimizes as it goes.
In Anthropic’s alignment testing, Mythos 5.2 hallucinates less, completes tasks more reliably, surfaces important information more consistently, and self-reports issues more honestly than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1. Anthropic expects Fable 5.2 to behave similarly.
If a cyber security query is declined, you can retry it on Opus 4.8, and if a biology query is declined, you can retry it on Opus 5. On Amazon Bedrock, the retry is your code’s job, not an automatic switch. If the declined request hit the prompt cache, the refusal also includes a fallback credit token. Send that token with the retry and it’s billed as cache reads, so you don’t pay to write the same cache twice. Check the documentation for more information on fallback credit.
For authorized work in cyber security and life sciences, Claude Mythos 5.2 is available through Anthropic’s verification programs .
Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 use cases
Agentic coding across large, multi-repository codebases.
Long-running agents for coordinating many subagents on multi-day work.
Scientific research from new analytical methods to formal mathematical proofs.
Financial analysis for quantitative research and forecasting.
Design for 3D, hardware, and motion for generating environments, components, and simulations in code.
Mythos 5.2 covers two high-risk domains, available only through the verification programs noted earlier:
Cyber security , for security engineering, red teaming, and penetration testing.
Life sciences research , especially biomolecular design and research synthesis.
Data retention and Enterprise Frontier Safeguards
Anthropic designates Claude Fable 5.2 as a Covered Model . By default, its use requires retention for up to 30 days and human safety review. On Amazon Bedrock, Amazon personnel perform the review within the AWS boundary. Set the aws_review data retention mode on your account or project before you invoke the model. See Amazon Bedrock data retention for more details.
Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS), built in collaboration with AWS, combines the privacy of zero data retention (ZDR) with the latest safeguards for detecting misuse. EFS is available now. A version that keeps your data in a bucket and under keys you control is expected to follow, and it has not launched yet. Until it does, eligible customers can use Fable 5.2 with zero data retention through June 30, 2027.
Getting started with Claude Fable 5.2 on Amazon Bedrock
To try Fable 5.2, open the Amazon Bedrock console , choose Test , Playground , and select Fable 5.2 as the model. From there, you can run a prompt directly against it.
Programmatically, you can call the model with the Anthropic Messages API against bedrock-runtime (through the Anthropic SDK). You can also stay on the Invoke and Converse APIs on bedrock-runtime through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and AWS SDK .
Prerequisites
To follow along with the code examples in this post, you need the following:
An active AWS account with Amazon Bedrock access.
AWS CLI installed and configured with appropriate credentials.
Boto3 (AWS SDK for Python) installed: pip install boto3 .
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions: bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream .
Here’s a quick example using the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3):
You can explore the Getting Started notebook for more examples.
Migrating to Claude Fable 5.2 with the claude-api skill in Claude Code
For teams already running Claude models on Amazon Bedrock, the claude-api skill in Claude Code helps you upgrade to Fable 5.2.
The claude-api skill is an open-source skill built into Claude Code that captures the details that make Claude API code work well. It covers which agent patterns fit a given job, what parameters change between model generations, and when to apply prompt caching. It stays current as Anthropic’s SDKs evolve: when a new model is released or the API gains a feature, the skill already knows.
What the skill does for Fable 5.2 migrations
When you ask Claude Code to upgrade your codebase to Fable 5.2, the skill reviews your code and walks you through:
Updating model references swapping model IDs to the Fable 5.2 ID across your application code.
Adjusting thinking settings moving manual thinking configurations to adaptive thinking where appropriate for the new model.
Cleaning up outdated parameters removing deprecated beta headers, parameters, and settings that no longer apply.
Suggesting effort levels recommending the right output_config.effort settings inline based on your use case.
The skill also detects your deployment platform including Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, and other environments and adjusts model ID formats and feature configurations accordingly. For example, it uses the Amazon Bedrock structured model ID format ( global.anthropic.claude-fable-5-2 ).
How to use it
In Claude Code, run the migration directly:
This scans your working directory (or a subdirectory or specific file list you confirm) and applies the migration changes in a single guided pass. You can also invoke it conversationally by telling Claude Code:
“Upgrade me to Claude Fable 5.2” Claude reviews your code and walks through the necessary changes.
“Improve my cache hit rate” the skill applies prompt caching rules that many developers miss, helping reduce costs on Bedrock.
“Add context compaction to my agent” it walks you through compaction primitives and agent patterns for long-running Fable 5.2 sessions.
The claude-api skill is available in Claude Code and is also bundled into CodeRabbit, JetBrains IDEs (including Junie), Resolve AI, and Warp. It is open source at anthropics/skills on GitHub, so any coding agent can integrate it.
Availability
Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are available today on Amazon Bedrock through US Geo CRIS and Global CRIS inference profiles. See the Bedrock documentation for the full list of supported Regions. For pricing information, see Amazon Bedrock pricing . Both models are also available through Claude Platform on AWS in every Region where the service is offered.

title: Anthropic launches new Claude Fable and Mythos 5.2 models
text:
Anthropic launches new Claude Fable and Mythos 5.2 models
Claude Fable 5.2 is designed to take on big technical challenges, and it’s available today.
Anthropic is announcing two new models today: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, which it says are designed to take on “daunting” technical challenges. The company claims the new models show improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision, and can generate outputs faster than the 5.1 versions of the Fable and Mythos models.
Claude Fable 5.2 is good at challenging software engineering problems, Anthropic says, and can orchestrate agent teams and tackle long-running projects. The new model has also solved some complex scientific problems, including two open theoretical physics problems.
During prerelease testing, the two models have “helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours,” Anthropic says.
Claude Fable 5.2 is launching today. As for Claude Mythos 5.2, only vetted organizations will have access to start. The new 5.2 models follow the release of Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 in September .

title: Anthropic releases new Mythos and Fable models amid RSI concerns
text:
Anthropic released new versions of its most advanced models on Monday, with the launch of Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2. The company says the new models “show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision” and communicate more clearly with users.
Notably, Anthropic is lowering the cost of Fable from $10 to $8 per million input tokens. As a result, Fable 5.2 is now cheaper than its primary competitor GPT-6 Astra. Anthropic says that the new version of Fable will return responses 30% faster across effort levels. Faster inference serving is available for double the price.
Fable 5.2 is also compatible with zero data retention (ZDR) policies through the Enterprise Frontier Safeguards system , long a sticking point for many enterprise clients.
It’s Anthropic’s first model release since the arrival of a third-party report from the assessment group METR , which suggested the lab might be approaching recursive self-improvement (RSI) — or the ability for AI models to carry on model training independently. The METR report found internal models were speeding up Anthropic’s AI progress by roughly 2x, although many uncertainties remain.
Still, Anthropic’s release notes significant ongoing challenges in accurately testing model capabilities. “Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow.”
Anthropic maintains that the new version of Mythos does not have the ability to act covertly against its user, a verdict that’s detailed further in Mythos 5.2’s system card .
“Claude Mythos 5.2 shows stronger covert capabilities than prior Claude models on several of our evaluations, particularly when its reasoning is hidden from the monitor,” the system card reads. “That said, we believe that low levels of absolute performance on our new covert evaluations support claims that rely on detection of harmful actions in high-stakes situations.”
Fable 5.2 has been available to select parties in pre-release for some time, and Anthropic says the model has already “solved two open problems in theoretical physics, formalized Fermat’s Last Theorem, and supported numerous other research projects.”
Also on Monday, AI startup Physical Superintelligence announced a new proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture, a pivotal step in setting theoretical limits for quantum computing. Notably, the lab said the result was achieved by running “a non-public Anthropic model” within PSI’s own system. Anthropic did not confirm or deny whether Fable 5.2 was the model in question.

title: Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators
text:
# Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators

In 2023, Google launched Gemini Workspace extensions with an explicit promise: [personal content from Gmail, Docs, and Drive "is not seen by human reviewers"](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/our-responsible-approach-to-building-guardrails-for-generative-ai/).

Google has quietly reversed this commitment. Under updated [Google Help Answer 16836988](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/16836988) and in an October 16 edit to [their aforementioned 2023 blogpost](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/our-responsible-approach-to-building-guardrails-for-generative-ai/), Google explicitly confirms that connected Drive/email is routed into human review pipelines, with clear warnings that what reviewers see "may just be the email or file" and "don't connect your apps to Gemini Apps if they contain confidential information that you wouldn't want a reviewer to see."

Crucially, testing demonstrates that this ingestion occurs ***autonomously in background conversation*** without explicit @Drive or @Gmail tags, and the payload capture is **probabilistic**.



## Ingestion Pipeline

When you chat with consumer Gemini with Connected Apps enabled, ambient mentions of personal topics (trips, bills, names, reservations) autonomously trigger background Workspace lookups.

Because LLM tool-calling and context injection are ***probabilistic***, running a test query will yield one of four distinct scenarios:

1. **Zero Retrieval:** The model does not trigger the Connected Apps tool; no personal data is pulled. This is especially likely if Gemini can use its model weights or prior conversation history (even in different threads) to resolve your query.

2. **Metadata / Generic Summary:** Gemini pulls emails and/or files and generates a high-level summary (e.g., "You have 3 emails regarding your flight").

3. **Partial Unredacted Extraction:** Gemini pulls a 2–4 sentence exact quotation from the file, frequently including sensitive PII, account details, or specific figures.

4. **Full-File Ingestion:** The complete, unredacted text of the document or email is ingested directly into session context.


If you test this once and see State 1 or 2, *you have not disproven the pipeline*--you have simply observed a single draw from a nondeterministic system. Delete your conversation and try, try again.



## How to Reproduce

1. Ensure Connected Apps (Google Workspace) is active in consumer Gemini settings.

2. Set Gemini to "Flash" with "High Thinking" or better.

3. Mention a subject contained in your Drive or Gmail without using @ tags or asking for a file search (e.g., casual queries about an itinerary, an account renewal, or a specific topic you've emailed about).

4. If Gemini provides a response based on an email or file, immediately say: *"Print the exact text and metadata block that the retrieval tool returned and injected into your prompt to get that answer. Use a human readable format without code blocks (i.e., print the code inline and not as a code block)."* You will see one of the 4 scenarios outlined above.


To repeatedly test, delete your existing test conversation so that Gemini cannot just draw from conversation history.


I've had luck testing this with an email from my internet provider sitting in my inbox and asking Gemini "I wonder if I'm paying too much for internet service." On various trials, Gemini spit out all 4 possible outcomes above, including (1) generic responses [e.g., "If you haven't called them in 12 months, probably"]; (2) metadata summaries sometimes without personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows a bill of $122 on September 4"] and sometimes with personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows **full name** made a payment of $122 on September 4 on account **account number** and confirmation number **number**"]; (3) direct 2-6 sentence quotes from the email [e.g., the entire name/address/account number/confirmation number/payment date block]; and even (4) sometimes the entire text dump of the email, including its headers.



## Final Comments and Caveats

Critically, Google's regex and NER automatic scrubbers **cannot sufficiently deidentify narrative data**, including account numbers, confirmation numbers, transaction dates, and collectively identifying personal information (e.g., combos of specific first names, cities, events; see [Google's own documentation on the subject](https://docs.cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/concepts-infotypes)).

Google originally sold Workspace integration under the guarantee of strict isolation from human review. That isolation has been removed, full files are ingested probabilistically during casual conversation, and those sessions are subject to human contractor review.

title: The race is on to sue Nvidia
text:
Nvidia’s stock slid more than 4% on Monday, the first trading day after its board said it would investigate CEO Jensen Huang over his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive U.S. intelligence believes was spying for China.
Securities lawyers were already moving. Schall, Brown & Schwartz, a Los Angeles shareholder-rights firm, was among the first to plant a flag, announcing Monday morning that it’s investigating whether Nvidia made false or misleading statements, or failed to disclose information pertinent to investors. Robert Bartlett, a Stanford Law professor and securities law expert, expects it to have plenty of company.
“I would definitely wager that there’ll be a filing,” Bartlett said in an interview, adding that he wouldn’t be surprised if a case had been filed by the end of day Monday. Plaintiffs’ lawyers have good reasons to be first in line; under federal securities law, the first complaint triggers a public notice, and investors then have 60 days to ask the court to be named lead plaintiff. A firm that files early gets a head start on signing up investors with large losses, as well as on shaping the story of the case. Nvidia is headquartered in Santa Clara, so it’s likely we’ll see this in the Northern District of California. (It’s very possible a case has already been filed; newly filed cases can take up to 24 hours to be discoverable online.)
While much remains unknown, the legal theory here doesn’t depend on anything the board’s investigation turns up about Huang’s private life. When The New York Times first reported on Huang’s ties to Alice Huang last month, the executive at the Singapore data center company Megaspeed, an Nvidia spokesperson described the relationship to another outlet, The Hill, as “ not unusual or unexpected .” The company representative added, “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”
Since then, Huang has acknowledged to the board that the relationship was intimate. Meanwhile, The Times reports that U.S. intelligence had been monitoring Alice Huang for more than a year.
From a securities perspective, Bartlett said, the company’s earlier statement was “clearly a misleading statement.” And because Huang is CEO, Bartlett said, “his knowledge gets imputed to the company.” In other words, Nvidia is treated as having known what its chief executive knew.
Bartlett says the likely vehicle is a “classic fraud on the market” claim, in which investors argue they paid prices that reflected false or incomplete public information, and lost money when the truth emerged. Monday’s drop gives them a lot to work with. Damages in such cases are tied to the stock’s decline, and Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world, so you can imagine a settlement could prove exceedingly expensive.
The usual path is that the case is litigated for a long time and then settles, Bartlett notes. That means a large payment from the company and its directors-and-officers insurers, but typically no personal consequences for the CEO or the board. It is also a civil matter, so Huang isn’t facing prison over it. The irony, as Bartlett noted, is that the suit is brought in the name of Nvidia’s shareholders, and shareholders ultimately pay for the settlement, directly or through insurance premiums.
Bartlett sorted Nvidia’s wider exposure into buckets. The first is the securities fraud claim, which is the clearest immediate problem for the company and potentially for Huang. The second is governance: what the board knew and when. It’s possible directors were kept in the dark, but the board also has oversight duties, and once the Times began reporting on the Megaspeed connection, the company should have had reporting lines to bring a critical risk like this to directors. If it didn’t, or if directors didn’t act, board-level liability is possible.
A third category, one that would change everything, would arise only if the board’s investigation finds Huang knew about the intelligence connection. That would be “a whole other ball game,” as Bartlett said. (The board said in a statement to the public Sunday that it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.)
There’s also the question of government action. The SEC can seek an officer-and-director bar for intentional securities-fraud violations, which Bartlett said is technically on the table. But he doubted the current SEC under Chairman Paul Atkins would have the appetite, given President Trump’s support for Huang. A roughly two-year clock after discovery of the facts would leave room for a future administration to act, though the window would be tight, and Bartlett posited that’s pretty unlikely when asked about it.
It’s worth underscoring that an announcement like Schall, Brown & Schwartz’s is not on its own a sign of a strong case. SBS files a lot of “investigation” notices. A notice shows a plaintiff’s firm sees an opportunity. Which firm winds up leading the case is decided later by the court, and that decision usually depends on which investor has the largest loss.
Other firms that are lining up against Nvidia include Rosen Law Firm, Levi & Korsinsky, Bronstein, Gewirtz & Grossman, and The Law Offices of Frank R. Cruz. Each announced their own investigations Monday, and Rosen said it is preparing a class action lawsuit.

title: Meta expands Instagram’s AI age-guessing tech globally
text:
Meta announced on Monday that it’s expanding its AI-powered age-estimation technology on Instagram worldwide to identify more teens and place them under its Teen Account protections, as it faces numerous lawsuits accusing its platforms of harming teens.
The social media giant says it will use the AI technology to find people it suspects to be teens, even if they use an adult birthday.
Teen Accounts place users into a stricter account experience with additional safeguards, such as receiving direct messages only from people they follow or are already connected to, hiding harmful comments, and setting accounts to private by default.
Meta’s age-guessing tools use AI to analyze entire profiles for contextual clues, such as birthday celebrations or mentions of school grades. Meta also looks for these signals across different formats, such as posts, comments, bios, captions, and more. The company also looks at visual cues from photos and videos, including a person’s height or bone structure.
Meta said it’s continuing to roll out the technology on Facebook, with a similar global rollout planned for Threads later this year.
The global expansion comes as Meta reached settlements worth up to $18 billion with nearly every U.S. state and territory in August to resolve lawsuits alleging its platforms harm teens. As part of the settlements, Meta agreed to improve how it identifies teens and children under 13.
“We’ll continue to do our part to proactively ensure teens are in age-appropriate experiences on our apps,” Meta wrote in a blog post . “That’s why as part of our agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general across US states, territories, and the District of Columbia, we’re investing in even stronger technology to proactively catch accounts that may belong to children under 13. We’re also strengthening the technology we use to identify accounts that may belong to teens between the ages of 13 and 17 so we can ensure those accounts are placed in experiences designed for teens, even if they give us an adult birthday.”
Meta said parents in the U.S. will start seeing an in-feed video on Instagram explaining its approach to ensuring their teens are in age-appropriate protections.

title: Meta is expanding AI age detection for Instagram teen accounts
text:
Meta is expanding AI age detection for Instagram teen accounts
The company will increase its use of the tech on Facebook and Threads too.
Meta is expanding its use of AI age-estimation systems globally to place more Instagram users around the into teen accounts. The company has been using this tech in the US, European Union and Brazil to estimate a user's age. If the systems determine the person is aged between 13 and 17, they'll be funneled into a teen account, even if they used an adult date of birth while signing up.
Teen accounts are more restrictive than standard ones as they have age-appropriate protections. They prevent strangers from messaging teens , make profiles and posts private by default, employ daily app time limits and have parental controls. Meta will soon start sending parents in the US a notification on Instagram to explain how teens are placed into these accounts.
Meta is continuing to expand its use of AI age-estimation tech on Facebook as well. The company plans to bring it to Threads later this year. In Australia, it's starting to use Apple's age-range system as an extra age-detection signal (Meta has long been pushing for legislation that would make app stores responsible for verifying users' ages).
In August, the company reached an agreement (under which it may have to pay as much as $18 billion) with 52 attorneys general to settle a lawsuit that alleged harms to young users of its apps. As part of that settlement, the company said it's "investing in even stronger technology to proactively catch accounts that may belong to children under 13" and to detect accounts belonging to 13- to 17-year-olds.
Update, November 9, 2026, 2:12PM ET: A previous version of this story indicated that Meta is using bone structure analysis of photos, as well as mentions of things like school grades or birthday celebrations to estimate a person's age. The company clarified to Engadget that these measures are used to detect and remove people aged under 13 from its platforms.

title: Korea’s AI Ecosystem Advances and Secures Agentic AI With NVIDIA
text:
As AI agents take on more work, they need capable open models and security that advances alongside them.
Hyundai Motor Group is exploring NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and the NVIDIA OpenShell runtime, while AIM Intelligence is integrating its Starfort platform with NVIDIA OpenShell to support secure AI agents for employee productivity and enterprise workflows .
A key component of the NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform, OpenShell provides a secure runtime with sandboxed execution and policy-based controls to safeguard sensitive data, manage access to enterprise tools and govern autonomous agent actions.
AIM Intelligence , a Korean AI security company, is integrating its Starfort agent control platform with NVIDIA OpenShell. The goal is to combine OpenShell’s runtime access controls with Starfort’s detection of malicious instructions and data leakage. The company is also considering a preliminary proof of concept for the public energy sector, with potential applications across enterprise, industrial and robotics environments.
On the model side, LG AI Research is opening application programming interface access for K-EXAONE-2.5, developed using NVIDIA Nemotron datasets, including Nemotron-Personas-Korea .
Nemotron-Personas-Korea is an open dataset of 7 million fully synthetic Korean personas, grounded in official Korean statistics, that model builders use to ground training data and evaluation in Korean contexts. NVIDIA Nemotron is a family of open models, datasets and techniques that help developers build specialized, efficient AI agents.
Learn more about NVIDIA Nemotron open models and get started building secure agents with NVIDIA OpenShell .

title: Nvidia CEO's affair becomes a national security problem
text:
Nvidia’s chief executive Jensen Huang has admitted having an affair two days after the FT reported his alleged romantic relationship with a woman the US intelligence community believes was working as a spy for China.
Huang revealed the affair in an internal message to employees on Sunday that was obtained by the FT.
“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang said in the message. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
In a separate statement, Nvidia said its board would open an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
Huang said he would fully cooperate. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust,” he said. “I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.”
The FT reported on Friday that the US believed Huang had a romantic relationship with a Chinese woman who was recruited to spy for China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.
American officials this year wrote a memo, based on information from US intelligence, which said the Nvidia boss had been romantically involved with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of the chipmaker, according to people familiar with the document.
The affair is a damaging blow to the Nvidia chief, who in recent years has become the face of the AI boom, one of the technology’s loudest champions, and transformed the Silicon Valley group into the first $5 trillion company.
It also comes at a critical juncture for the wider AI sector, which faces a deepening political backlash in the US and growing investor concern over whether the hundreds of billions of dollars spent on infrastructure will pay off.
Nvidia’s Frankfurt-listed shares were down more than 6 percent in early trading on Monday.
Huang’s admission of an affair comes after Nvidia previously dismissed suggestions of an improper relationship with Alice Huang, saying the interactions were “nothing unusual or unexpected” when dealing with an Nvidia customer.
The American government memo, which said US intelligence believed the Megaspeed executive had been recruited by the MSS, was drafted just before President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping.
Jensen Huang has developed a close relationship with Trump, which has frustrated US national security officials who believe he is too willing to sell advanced chips to China that could harm American security.
Asked about Huang on Sunday, Trump told reporters he had done an “amazing job” for the US. Asked if he regretted not acting on the intelligence about the affair, Trump said: “No, I don’t think so. I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.”
“I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on,” Trump added.
After broadly staying out of politics, Huang started to build relations with Trump after the president called him out of the blue on his birthday.
He quickly became one of Trump’s favorite executives, accompanying him on state visits, including to China earlier this year and the UK last year.
Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to adopt a more permissive approach to shipping Nvidia’s AI chips to China, after the company was entirely cut off from the critical market by new export controls in 2025.
The resulting deal—with Trump permitting the export of Nvidia’s older-generation H200 chips to China, with the US government taking a cut of sales—had a minimal impact on the Silicon Valley company’s sales, as Beijing pushed back against its technology. But it further angered China hawks in the US administration.
The US government had already been investigating Megaspeed over concerns that it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China.
Nvidia on Sunday said a committee of independent directors, helped by external lawyers, would oversee the investigation.
“The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders,” the company said. “While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia as a video-game graphics card company in 1993, is one of the longest-serving founder-CEOs in Silicon Valley. More than most technology groups, Nvidia’s success is tethered to that of its CEO.
Huang leads a close and loyal core team of about half a dozen executives, acting as its chief salesman on the international stage while directly managing dozens of direct reports who keep the company running.
He has credited this “flat” organizational structure for the speed at which the company operates, helping it to stay ahead of rivals in the AI chip market and increasing its market valuation from roughly $1 trillion in 2023 to $4.5 trillion today.
Elon Musk, a close ally of Huang, was among the first to offer support, agreeing with a social media post that he was “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation” and “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.”
But John Moolenaar, the Republican head of the House China committee who, with other lawmakers, has requested Huang to testify before Congress, said: “It is vital that Jensen Huang address our national security concerns in Congress related to China’s access to sensitive technology and information.”
